speaker_role: current admissions officer (Dean of Admissions at Yale Law School and Dean of Admissions at Harvard Law School)
commercial_incentive: The two guests host their own admissions podcast/brand (promoting listeners to it); no direct product sale in this episode
key_insights: This entire discussion is about LAW SCHOOL (graduate/professional) admissions at Harvard and Yale, not undergraduate admissions, so it is off-scope for this research base.

Deans note a growing majority of admits now apply several years after undergrad rather than straight through, citing an internal data point that incoming admits with 5+ years post-undergrad work experience outnumber those straight from college by roughly 3 to 1 at one school.
Deans state 'demonstrated interest' (campus visits, attending events) is much less influential in law school admissions than they believe it is in undergraduate admissions.

Deans describe evaluating three balanced factors: academic ability, community contribution, and collegiality/character, noting that top numerical scores alone are no longer a near-automatic admit given grade/test score inflation.

Deans state a very high GPA (e.g. 4.0) is not by itself reassuring, since it can mask low course rigor or weak letters, and that strong applicants with excellent work-experience narratives can outperform slightly higher-scoring peers.
Deans emphasize letters of recommendation should describe specific character and growth (e.g. how a student improved, listened, or contributed) rather than generic superlative praise.
Deans state failing to follow application instructions (e.g., word/page limits) is treated as a serious red flag reflecting poor professionalism.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Harvard Law dean: incoming class expected to have roughly 3x as many admits who are 5+ years out of undergrad as those applying straight from college
Deans reference median LSAT scores in the '160s to 170s' (90th percentile+) as typical for admitted students at these two schools
